name: Research Programmes
statement: Judge science not by single theories but by whether a whole programme keeps predicting new facts.
statementAccent: whether a whole programme keeps predicting new facts
meaning: The methodology of scientific research programmes is Imre Lakatos's account of scientific rationality, developed as an attempt to reconcile Karl Popper's falsificationism with Thomas Kuhn's account of scientific revolutions. Its central move is to change the unit of appraisal: instead of judging isolated theories, one by one, against the evidence, Lakatos judges research programmes, sequences of related theories that develop over time. A research programme has a definite structure. At its center is the hard core, the fundamental theoretical assumptions that define the programme and that its practitioners treat as irrefutable by methodological decision, so that refutations are not directed at the core; Lakatos called this rule the negative heuristic. Surrounding the hard core is a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses, which bears the brunt of testing and is adjusted, modified, and elaborated in response to anomalies, shielding the core. Guiding this work is the positive heuristic, a set of suggestions and hints for how to develop the programme and build up the protective belt. Programmes are appraised as progressive or degenerating: a programme is progressive when its modifications predict novel facts, some of which are confirmed, and degenerating when its modifications are merely ad hoc patches that accommodate known anomalies without predicting anything new. Science is rational, on this view, when it pursues progressive programmes.
mechanism: Lakatos's methodology works by appraising the track record of a whole programme rather than the fate of a single theory. The hard core states the programme's defining commitments, and the negative heuristic forbids aiming refutations at it; when the programme meets anomalies, the modus tollens is directed instead at the protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses, which is revised, extended, or replaced to absorb the anomaly and keep the core intact. This answers the Duhem-Quine problem, that logic alone does not say which assumption to blame, by having the programme's own methodological rules decide: the core is protected, the belt is adjusted. The positive heuristic supplies a plan for these adjustments, telling researchers which models to build next and which complications to add, so that the programme develops in a directed way rather than by improvised rescue. The crucial evaluation is dynamic and historical. A programme is theoretically progressive if each new version predicts some novel, unexpected fact, and empirically progressive if some of those predicted facts are then confirmed; it is degenerating if its changes only mop up known difficulties after the fact, without leading to new predictions. Because appraisal tracks whole sequences over time, a programme is not abandoned at the first anomaly, which accommodates Kuhn's observation that scientists persist through difficulties, while progress and degeneration give a rational standard for preferring one programme to another, preserving the Popperian demand for empirical content and testable predictions.

examples.text: The programme's defining assumptions form a hard core, shielded by a protective belt of auxiliaries that absorbs anomalies.
A programme is progressive when its modifications predict novel facts that are later confirmed, not merely patched to fit.
A programme degenerates when it only adds ad hoc rescues to accommodate known anomalies without predicting anything new.

variants.name: Sophisticated falsificationism
variants.text: Lakatos's appraisal of whole sequences of theories, replacing the naive falsification of isolated theories.

whyItMatters: Lakatos's methodology of scientific research programmes is one of the major twentieth-century attempts to say what makes science rational, and it occupies a crucial middle position between Popper and Kuhn. Against Popper's naive falsificationism, it recognizes that scientists rightly do not abandon a promising theory at the first anomaly, and it locates rationality in the developing track record of a programme rather than in the instant refutation of a single hypothesis. Against the apparent irrationalism some read into Kuhn, it supplies an objective standard, progress versus degeneration, by which competing programmes can be rationally compared, without pretending that theory choice is a mechanical algorithm. Its vocabulary, the hard core, the protective belt, the positive and negative heuristics, and progressive and degenerating programmes, has become a standard toolkit for describing how real research traditions grow, stall, and are superseded, and it is widely applied beyond physics, in economics, psychology, and the social sciences, to assess whether a field is making genuine progress. Lakatos also offered a distinctive account of the history of science as a rational reconstruction.

working.text: appraise a research programme, a sequence of theories over time, rather than an isolated theory.
shield the hard core by directing revisions at the protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses.
count the programme progressive if its changes predict confirmed novel facts, degenerating if they only patch anomalies.

limits: Lakatos's methodology faces real objections, several concerning its practical bite and its treatment of time. The distinction between progressive and degenerating programmes is only reliably applied in retrospect: a programme that looks degenerating may later revive with a burst of novel predictions, so at any given moment the methodology may not tell scientists which programme to pursue or when to abandon one, and Lakatos allowed that it can be rational to stick with a temporarily degenerating programme. This makes the account arguably better as a standard for evaluating the history of science after the fact than as a guide to live decisions. The notion of a novel fact, on which the appraisal turns, is itself contested and admits several interpretations. The decision to protect a particular hard core is a methodological convention that critics say can shade into dogmatism, and identifying the core and belt of a real programme is not always straightforward. Some datings and attributions, such as the 1970 paper and the 1978 posthumous Philosophical Papers, reward checking.
misreadings: The methodology of research programmes does not say a programme should be dropped at the first anomaly; it protects the hard core and judges the programme over time. Progressive and degenerating are not verdicts about a single theory but about a developing sequence, and a degenerating phase need not mean immediate abandonment. And the account is not a mechanical algorithm for theory choice, since it may deliver clear verdicts only in retrospect, so treating it as demanding instant abandonment, as appraising lone theories, or as an automatic decision procedure, misreads Lakatos's methodology.
origin: Imre Lakatos's account of scientific rationality, set out in his 1970 paper and 1978 Philosophical Papers, appraising research programmes, with a hard core, protective belt, and heuristics, as progressive or degenerating.
